title: Skin to Skin for Premature Babies
text:
Premature babies usually spend their first weeks in incubators, which keep them warm and safe but separate them from their parents' bodies. Kangaroo care, first promoted in Colombia in the late 1970s, offers an alternative: the baby, wearing only a diaper, is held upright against the parent's bare chest.

Ruth Feldman, a developmental psychologist and neuroscientist at Bar-Ilan University in Israel, and her colleagues Zehava Rosenthal and Arthur Eidelman studied its long-term effects. In a neonatal intensive care unit, mothers of 73 premature infants provided skin-to-skin contact for an hour a day over fourteen consecutive days. These babies were compared with 73 premature babies matched on factors such as birth weight and medical condition, who received standard incubator care.

The team then followed the children for ten years, assessing them seven times. At age ten, the children who had received kangaroo care showed more mature physiological regulation: better organized sleep, a more flexible heart rate pattern linked to calm and attention, and a healthier hormonal response to stress. They also performed better on tests of cognitive control, such as focusing attention and holding back impulses. Their mothers had been more sensitive in interactions with them during the early years.

Fourteen hours of touch in the first weeks of life were associated with differences a decade later.
lesson: Touch is a form of care with lasting power. Holding a baby close, skin to skin, does real work for the body and the mind.
people: Ruth Feldman, Zehava Rosenthal, Arthur Eidelman
source: Feldman, R., Rosenthal, Z., and Eidelman, A. I. (2014). Maternal-preterm skin-to-skin contact enhances child physiologic organization and cognitive control across the first 10 years of life. Biological Psychiatry, 75(1), 56-64.
caveat: Mothers were not randomly assigned to kangaroo care, so other differences between the groups may have played a role.
